bio.en: Sam Schillace is Corporate Vice President and Deputy CTO at Microsoft, leading consumer product, infrastructure, and AI efforts, and is best known for essentially inventing Google Docs with his company Writely.
bio.zh: Sam Schillace 是微软公司副总裁兼副首席技术官（Deputy CTO），领导消费级产品、基础设施与 AI 方面的工作；他最为人知的成就是凭借自己的公司 Writely 几乎凭一己之力发明了 Google Docs。

summary.en: Sam shares a framework for spotting disruptive innovation: if some people love it and many hate it, it's probably disruptive, whereas broadly 'meh' reactions signal it isn't. He tells the Google Docs origin story and argues that everything around us was once a threatening disruptive idea, so we should expect new ideas to look 'dumb' at first. The conversation also covers first-principles thinking and why undervaluing what comes easily is a career trap.
summary.zh: Sam 分享了一个识别颠覆性创新的框架：如果一部分人狂热喜爱、而许多人强烈厌恶，那它很可能具有颠覆性；相反，若普遍反应平淡，则往往不是。他讲述了 Google Docs 的起源故事，并主张我们周遭的一切都曾是“令人不安的颠覆性想法”，因此应当预期新点子一开始看起来“很蠢”。对话还涉及第一性原理思维，以及为何低估“得来容易之事”是职业陷阱。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: We tend to undervalue the things we're good at. We tend to think work has to be unpleasant. And so if something is easy and fun, we don't tend to think it's valuable. So I think lots of people gravitate in this direction of like, let's go do unpleasant things and grind our way through the career because that's the way to make it. But the reality is you should go do the thing that you feel guilty to get paid for, if there's a thing like that, and do the hell out of it, right? Do it as hard as you can. If you get pleasure from doing something that people want to pay you for, do it the best you can do it, as hard as you can do it. And if that's messing around and playing around with cool ideas, do the hell out of that. Work doesn't necessarily have to be hard.
turns.zh: 我们往往低估了自己擅长的事物。我们总认为工作就该是令人不快的。所以如果某件事既简单又有趣，我们往往不会认为它有价值。因此，我认为很多人都倾向于这样一种观念：去干那些不愉快的工作，靠死磕才能在事业上有所成就。但现实是，如果有某件事让你觉得自己不配从中获利，那就大胆去干，尽全力做到最好。若你能从人们愿意为之付费的事情中获得乐趣，那就全力以赴地做到极致。即便那只是随心所欲地探索酷炫创意，也要尽情享受这个过程。工作不一定要很艰难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A really fun fact about you is that apparently you have the very first Google Doc file. I don't know what you call it. The very first Google Doc document saved somewhere from before even Google Docs was a thing. And does it still work in today's Google Docs? And what is in this document?
turns.zh: 关于你的一件趣事是，显然你拥有首个Google Doc文件。我不知道你们怎么称呼它。早在Google Docs诞生之前，就有一个保存的文档。它在如今的Google Docs中还能正常使用吗？文件内容是什么？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, it does actually still work. It's pretty funny. Actually, if I move my camera for a second you might, if you're on YouTube, you can see the Writely thing in the background. Writely was the company that did Google Docs. Yeah, it still works. And it's funny though because it's like the document of DCS, right? So we started off 2005, wrote this thing in C#, which is a little known, in our own... It was pre-cloud, so we had three file servers that we rented that were Windows machines in a data center in Texas with a sysadmin in the Philippines running them. So it started there. (00:04:43): And then when we moved to Google, we ported everything to Java, we moved all the data over into Bigtable. And we didn't lose anything. We never lost anybody's stuff. So it's still there and moved across. And then so that's one backend migration, and there's another one with Spanner. And then the front end has been rewritten twice as well. So it's like, is it really the same document? I don't know. The front end, back end have been rewritten. It's not much. It's just me saying something to Steve about, is collaboration working? Are we colliding on each other? Because we were trying to figure out typing on one line, if that algorithm was working. (00:05:14): And then there's a picture of Edna from The Incredibles pasted into it. I don't know why. I think that came after, so I might've gone back and pasted that in. I'm not sure when. We must've been testing pictures or something. Unfortunately, we don't have the version history anymore, so I don't know what was original, original. But it is the oldest Google Doc from October 2005 or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的，它确实还能用。挺有意思的。其实如果我把镜头移过去一秒，你们在YouTube上可能会看到背景里的Writely界面。Writely就是开发Google Docs的公司。没错，它还能用。挺有意思的，因为这应该是DCS的文档吧？我们2005年就开始了，用C#编写，当时这门语言鲜为人知，用我们自己的服务器——那还是云计算时代之前的事。我们在德克萨斯州的数据中心租了三台Windows服务器，由菲律宾的系统管理员负责维护。就从那里起步了。（00:04:43）后来迁移到Google平台时，我们把所有代码移植到Java平台，把数据迁移到Bigtable里，没有丢失任何数据。我们从未丢失过用户资料。所以这些数据都完整迁移过来了。然后还有一次迁移到Spanner，再后来前端也重写了两次。所以现在还算不算同一个文档？我不知道。前后端都改过好几次了。其实差别不大。我只是在和Steve讨论协作功能是否正常，避免互相冲突，因为我们当时在测试一行代码的输入算法是否有效。（00:05:14）然后里面还插入了《超人总动员》中埃德娜的图片，不知道为什么。我觉得那是后来加的，我也不确定具体时间。我们当时可能在测试图片功能。可惜现在没有版本历史记录了，所以不知道原始内容是什么。不过这个文件确实是2005年10月左右的最早版本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that this philosophical answer of, is it still the same Google Doc, considering all the code has been redone.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种哲学式的讨论：考虑到代码都重写了，它还是同一个Google Doc吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Well, the Computer History Museum wants to curate it. I talked to these guys and they were like, "Oh, that's so cool. We'll take that." I'm like, "How?" I can make you a PDF. Now it's not the document. I can share you into it, but please don't edit it. How do you curate this? So that's funny.
turns.zh: 嗯，计算机历史博物馆想把它收藏起来。我和他们聊过，他们说"太棒了，我们要收录这个。"我问"怎么做？"我可以把它做成PDF，但那不是原始文件。我可以让你们访问，但请勿编辑。你们怎么收藏？挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It needs to be on the blockchain.
turns.zh: 是啊。这东西得上区块链。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. If you made the NFT of it, that would be more authentic, I think, than the document almost. It's kind of funny.
turns.zh: 对。对。如果把它做成NFT，应该比原始文件更具真实性吧。这挺有意思的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. And it's amazing that it still works. That's a testament to, I don't know, you/Google.
turns.zh: 太神奇了。它还能用真是不可思议。这充分证明了……我不知道，是你/Google的实力吧。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Well, I'll tell you a quick Google story. When we migrated in to Google, we were very sneaky about it, and we put the site into "maintenance mode" for eight hours on a Sunday, where everything was just read-only. And then we migrated all the data and moved everything and brought the new system up. And three days after that, Sergei was in a meeting with me and he's like, "So when are you guys going to move over to Google infrastructure?" And I got to tell them, "Oh yeah, we did it this weekend." No one noticed. Some blogger in Germany noticed that the IP address changed and that was it. Nobody noticed it at all, so we were really good about it.
turns.zh: 嗯，我来给你们讲个谷歌的趣事。当时我们迁移到谷歌平台时，采取了非常隐蔽的策略。周日那天，我们把网站置于“维护模式”八小时，期间所有内容都处于只读状态。然后我们迁移了所有数据，完成所有操作并启用新系统。三天后，谢尔盖和我开会时他问：“你们什么时候迁移到谷歌基础设施啊？”我不得不告诉他：“哦，对了，我们这周末就完成了。” 结果没人察觉。德国某位博主发现IP地址变了，仅此而已。根本没人发现问题，所以我们这次做得非常隐蔽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, I love these sneaky stories. I'm hoping we hear more. There's a bunch of stuff I want to cover, the first is this broad idea of disruptive innovation. I know that you spend a lot of time thinking about this. Google Docs is a great example of this. It feels like Microsoft increasingly is getting really good at this. Just the idea of doing something completely new, oftentimes things that people didn't think were possible. So let me just ask a broad question. Why is this important to you? Why do you spend a lot of time thinking about this? And then just what are some tools you've found to help you and other people think more innovatively, more originally?
turns.zh: 天哪，我超爱这些隐蔽行动的故事。希望能听到更多类似趣闻。接下来我想探讨一下颠覆性创新这个宏观概念。我知道你们花了大量时间思考这个问题。谷歌文档就是一个绝佳范例。感觉微软在这方面也越来越擅长了。就是创造全新的东西，往往是人们认为不可能实现的创新。那么我来问个开放性问题：为什么这对你们如此重要？为什么你们要花大量时间研究这个？还有，你们发现了哪些工具能帮助自己和他人更具创新性、更富有创造力？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: It's an interesting question. The why it's important part, I don't know, it just is. Everything you're wearing, eating, using, listening to, sitting on, was a disruptive innovation at some point. That's how everything happens, right? I think there's this really interesting thing where everything new is threatening at some level at the beginning. I mean, probably literally the first guy who invented chairs got shit from his tribe mates for making a chair. And they're all obvious in retrospect, right? Everything is obvious in retrospect. (00:07:51): But I think there's this really deep thing that people have where if something is disruptive of your worldview, it feels threatening, and you have this very stark choice to make that's either you're wrong or it's wrong. And humans are storytellers. It's very easy for us to tell stories about why something is right or wrong if we're motivated to. And so I call these why-not questions. People ask these why-not questions a lot. So a new thing pops up, and if you're not ready to receive it for some reason, you're not already half there or you don't have a problem that it solves or whatever, it's just threatening and irritating, and you come up with a why-not question. (00:08:29): We heard a bunch of these with Google Docs, with Writely, in the early days about the browser wasn't ready, people wouldn't... The whole model of the cloud was like, people aren't going to trust you to store your files. That's really weird. What if there's no connectivity? I heard the no connectivity on an airplane story 100 times from journalists. Like, "What if I'm on an airplane and I write stuff?" I'm like, "I don't know. There'll be connectivity on airplanes soon." Which there is. And those are all just why-not questions. (00:08:55): I think the more interesting ones are the what-if questions, like, what if this does work? Just use your imagination. Think about, how far can I extend the curve? What are the implications of that? I'm an engineer, and engineers are fundamentally pessimistic people. Somebody once told me engineers come into the world broken. They just look at everything as a problem to be solved. And I think there's something to that. But I feel like I've missed out more by being pessimistic than I have by being too optimistic too early. (00:09:26): So I have this kind of mantra now that there's just not that much of a prize for being pessimistic and right, particularly in a moment like this. It's much better to be optimistic and wrong than pessimistic and right, I think. So I don't know. And I'm an impatient person. I'm a creative person. I'm a messy person. I just like to create and explore and find stuff. So disruptive innovation just seems natural to me. But I think it's not an exaggeration to say, literally, that wheat you had in your bread this morning, if you eat bread, some weirdo was messing around with plants 1,000 years ago and everybody thought he was a nut, or she was a nut, and then we had wheat because somebody... Just everything, right? Everything is like that.
turns.zh: 这是个很有趣的问题。至于为什么它重要，我也不知道，就是这样。你们现在穿的衣服、吃的食物、用的工具、听的音乐、坐的椅子，在某个时候都曾是颠覆性的创新。一切事物的发生不都是如此吗？我觉得有个很有意思的现象：每种新事物在刚出现时都会被视为威胁。比如，第一个发明椅子的人可能就被部落同伴嘲笑了。但事后看来，一切都显而易见。（00:07:51）但我认为人们内心深处有个观念：如果某件事挑战了你的世界观，就会觉得它威胁到了你。这时你就得做个艰难的选择——要么承认自己错了，要么承认它错了。而人类天生就是讲故事的高手，只要有动机，我们就能轻易编造出某种事物正确或错误的理由。我把这类问题称为"为什么不"问题。人们经常问这种问题。当新事物出现时，如果你因为某些原因还没准备好接受它——比如你还没有半个心思去迎接它，或者它解决不了你的问题等等——它就会显得威胁大、令人不快，于是你就会提出"为什么不"的问题。（00:08:29）我们在谷歌文档、Writely等产品早期就听过很多类似的抱怨：浏览器还没准备好，人们不会用……整个云存储模式被认为人们不会信任你存储文件。这真的很奇怪。要是没网络连接怎么办？记者们把"飞机上没网络"的故事讲了无数遍。比如"我在飞机上写东西怎么办？"我说"我不知道。很快飞机上就会有网络了。"现在确实有了。这些都是"为什么不"的问题。（00:08:55）我觉得更有趣的是"假如……会怎样"的问题。比如，假如这真的可行呢？发挥想象力。想想看，我能把曲线延伸多远？这会带来什么影响？我是个工程师，工程师天生就是悲观主义者。有人曾说工程师生来就带有缺陷。他们把一切都视为需要解决的问题。我觉得这话有道理。但我觉得过早地过于乐观比过于悲观带来的损失更大。（00:09:26）所以我现在有这样一个信念：悲观并正确并没有多大好处，尤其是在当下这样的时刻。乐观并错误总比悲观并正确要好得多。所以我不知道。我是个没耐心的人。我是个有创造力的人。我是个做事不拘小节的人。我就是喜欢创造、探索和发现新事物。所以颠覆性创新对我来说很自然。但我觉得毫不夸张地说，如果你今天早餐吃的面包里的麦子，是1000年前某个怪人摆弄植物种出来的——那又怎样？一切都是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, I was actually just working on a post around first-principles thinking. And I found this quote from Steve Jobs just reminding us that everything around us was designed by some person that wasn't necessarily that much smarter than you. And there's no reason there isn't a better way. It just happens to be the way it is today.
turns.zh: 同样，我最近刚在写一篇关于第一性原理思维的文章。我发现了史蒂夫·乔布斯的一句话，他提醒我们，身边的一切都是由某个并不比你聪明太多的人设计的。没有理由认为不存在更好的方法。只是现在事情就是这样。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah. One of the other ones that I like to keep in mind is every new idea looks dumb at first. Unfortunately, the dumb ideas also look dumb at first. It's not a perfect [inaudible 00:10:35]. But the more disruptive they are, the more dumb you're going to feel they are. You always listen for stuff like if they say it's a toy or if it's practical or it's stupid or I don't get it or whatever, those are often... Toy is a good keyword. If you hear people saying something's a toy, that's often a really good signifier that it's actually something real and threatening, and they can't think of a better criticism for it than it's just a toy right now.
turns.zh: 是啊。我还想起另一个我常记在心里的观点：每个新想法一开始看起来都很蠢。可惜，愚蠢的想法一开始看起来也很蠢。这并不完美（00:10:35处语音不清）。但它们越具颠覆性，你就越会觉得它们很蠢。你总会留意一些关键信号，比如他们说这是个玩具、实用还是愚蠢，或者“我不明白”之类的。这些关键词通常很管用。如果他们说这是个玩具，那通常意味着这东西确实很真实、很具威胁性，而他们找不到比“这只是个玩具”更贴切的批评了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I imagine people thought about Google Docs that way initially. It was like, "Oh, this little toy in the browser."
turns.zh: 是啊，我想人们最初对Google Docs也是这么看的。他们会说：“哦，这只是浏览器里的一个小玩具。”

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, we got all this stuff. I mean, the real interesting thing, like I said at the beginning, you have this very binary reaction that's possible, right? You either understand it, in which case, you're super excited about it like, "Cool, the world's going to change in this exciting way." Or you don't and you reject it. And to the degree that something is really disruptive, that reaction, that binary reaction gets really strong. And so with something like G Docs, we got this thing with G Docs that was really confusing in the early days to me, where there was a small group of people that really liked it. Some of them liked it more than we liked it. Nate Torkington over at Writely was this super huge early booster for it. And I did not understand what he saw in it at first. But then we had people that just wanted it to die in a fire. (00:11:52): And that bifurcation of love it, hate it, is really how you have an idea of whether you have impact in what you're building. If you get more of the bell curve of modern indifference and maybe mild like and mild dislike, that's an's an incremental product. That's not really disrupting anything. But if you look at something like ChatGPT where the entire world is like, "This is amazing." Or, "This is terrible." And there's not a whole lot in between, that's a very good signifier of it being truly impactful and disruptive. Whether it's actually good or bad is a separate question. But there's no denying that that's a disruptive technology.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们遇到过各种情况。我在开头说过，人们对新事物可能有两种极端反应：要么你理解它，兴奋不已，觉得“太棒了，世界要因此迎来激动人心的变革”；要么你不理解，就直接否定它。而当某个东西真的具有颠覆性时，这种二元反应就会变得极其强烈。比如G Docs早期就让我很困惑，有一小群人特别喜欢它，有些人甚至比我们更痴迷。Nate Torkington在Writely上就是它的狂热支持者，我一开始根本不明白他看中了它哪一点。但后来也有人恨不得它赶紧消失。（00:11:52）：这种爱恨分明的两极分化，是判断你所构建的东西是否有影响力的重要指标。如果得到的是现代版的“无感”和“轻微好感/轻微厌恶”的钟形曲线，那说明这只是个渐进式产品，根本没有颠覆性。但如果像ChatGPT这样全世界都在说“太棒了”或者“太可怕了”，中间几乎没有灰色地带，那就是真正有影响力、有颠覆性的标志。它到底是好是坏是另外的问题，但不可否认这是一项颠覆性技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome framework. Basically, if it feels like people sort of like it, mostly people don't care, very few people love it or hate it, probably not disruptive. If some people absolutely love it and a lot of people really hate it, good sign.
turns.zh: 这真是个绝妙的框架。基本上，如果人们看起来只是喜欢它，大多数人不关心它，喜欢或厌恶的人很少，那可能就没什么颠覆性。如果有人特别喜欢它，而很多人特别讨厌它，那就是个好迹象。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Right. Yeah. Actually, weirdly enough. It's not voting, right? In the early days, we had, I don't know, a couple of million users, five million users, and there were still executives at Google telling me that it was a stupid idea and that it should stop and we shouldn't be doing it. So, for a long time, the haters outnumbered the people who were fans. And who cares? Whatever. It's fine. As long as you don't run out of the people who love it, that's fine.
turns.zh: 对。没错。说来奇怪，这不是投票表决的问题。早期我们有几百万用户，五百万用户，但谷歌的高管们还是对我说这是个愚蠢的主意，应该停止开发。所以很长一段时间里，讨厌它的人比喜欢它的人多得多。但管他呢，随他去吧。只要喜欢它的人不减少，就没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there another example of you using this what-if approach either on a product you worked on or something you've seen and it working out?
turns.zh: 有没有其他例子，说明你用这种假设性思考方法，无论是在你参与过的产品上，还是在你见过的其他案例中，最后都取得了成功？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: I'm doing a lot of it right now, honestly. I mean, that's probably the most immediate example. But I could almost point at any product and there's moments like that in there. But right now there's a lot of why-not stories, right, around generative AI. So it's expensive, it hallucinates, you can't necessarily... It's sarcastic, it's random, it doesn't do the same thing twice. Yeah, they're real, they're actual issues to solve, but I look at it and think, "Well, what if? What if we can build software around it? What if we can build more complicated programs than what we've been able to build? What if we actually have a reasoning engine that we can use to do meaningful things? What if this is really the second Industrial Revolution where, in the first one, we had a surplus of physical energy beyond just our bodies and things like water reels, and now we have a surplus of cognitive energy beyond just our brains, right?" (00:14:17): And that's a really transformational idea. So I'm completely in that mode right now, honestly. I think that's just the right mindset for something that's obviously this disruptive, right or wrong. Tesla is a great example. SpaceX is a great example where people are like, "That doesn't make any sense." And Elon's like, "Well, what if you could land rockets and reuse them and they get really cheap? That's pretty amazing. What if I can fix the battery problems and a car is basically a software product, right?" Those are pretty amazing what-if questions, right, of those products.
turns.zh:
老实说，我现在正大量做这类事情。我的意思是，这可能是最直接的例子。但几乎任何产品都会有这样的时刻。不过现在，围绕生成式人工智能有很多"为什么不行"的质疑。比如它价格高昂、会产生幻觉、无法稳定输出……它很讽刺、随机无序、两次结果完全不同。是的，这些都是真实存在的、亟待解决的问题。但当我审视这些问题时，就会想："如果呢？如果我们能围绕它开发软件呢？如果我们能构建比现有复杂得多的程序呢？如果我们真能拥有一个能执行有意义任务的推理引擎呢？如果这真是第二次工业革命呢？第一次工业革命是人类利用超出自身的物理能量（比如水车），现在我们则是在开发超出大脑的认知能量。"
（00:14:17）这确实是个极具变革性的理念。所以说老实话，我现在完全处于这种状态。我认为对于如此颠覆性的技术，保持这种思维模式至关重要，无论它是对是错。特斯拉就是个绝佳例子，SpaceX也是个典型案例——人们会说："这根本说不通。"而埃隆会反问："那如果能让火箭着陆并重复使用，而且成本极低呢？这简直太棒了。如果能解决电池问题，让汽车成为纯软件产品呢？"这些"如果……会怎样"的问题，确实令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So in this work on understanding what first principles actually looks like when you're thinking from first principles, the steps are essentially, figure out what you want to do, figure out the levers that keep you from achieving that thing, and then basically question every assumption that stands in the way of making this possible. So I think Elon's a great... The classic example. You can't talk about first-principles thinking without quoting Elon, telling stories of Elon. But essentially, it's just, okay, how much would it cost to make this if we were to start over and not...
turns.zh: 是的。在理解第一性原理的过程中，当你以第一性原理思考时，关键步骤本质上是，先明确你想做什么，找出阻碍你实现目标的因素，然后质疑所有阻碍的假设。所以我认为埃隆是个绝佳范例。谈论第一性原理思维时，人们总会引用埃隆的例子，讲述他的故事。但本质上，就是：如果从头开始重建，这个成本有多高？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: I mean, the why-nots, there are actually problems you need to pay attention to eventually to build stuff. But once you have the what-if, right, just to pick on SpaceX for a second, right? If you have what-if of like, "If I could make payload to space cost a lot less, what if?" Okay, that's amazing. That's an amazing world. Let's see if we can work on that problem. And then now you have all the why-nots? Why not? Why isn't it as cheap as it could be? And you can start to break the problem down and think about it that way. It's a good model.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，"为什么不行"的问题，最终都是构建产品时必须关注的难题。但一旦你有了"如果……会怎样"的思路，比如以SpaceX为例，如果能大幅降低太空载荷成本，那会怎样？好吧，这太棒了。这会创造一个惊人的世界。让我们看看能否攻克这个难题。然后现在就涌现出一堆"为什么不行"的问题。为什么不行？为什么成本达不到应有的低价？然后你可以分解问题，按照这种思路去思考。这是个很好的模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This connects to something else that I know you're big on, which is optimism, being optimistic. There's this feeling that pessimism, you're often right. There's growing pessimism in the world in a lot of ways, especially in technology. I know you're a big proponent of staying optimistic. Can you just talk about why you think that's important and how you approach that?
turns.zh: 这与我知道你特别推崇的乐观主义思维模式相关。人们常说，悲观主义者往往是对的。但在很多方面，尤其是在科技领域，全球悲观情绪日益加剧。我知道你非常支持保持乐观。你能谈谈为什么你认为这很重要，以及你是如何做到的吗？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: It's funny, it's a choice. I'm not an optimistic person by nature. I'm just not. All the people in my life, if any of them listen to this, they'll just laugh at the idea that I'm a proponent for optimism per se. It's just a conscious choice. I don't think you get very much for being pessimistic necessarily. You definitely don't get a lot for being careless. You can be optimistic to the point of being careless and causing harm, for sure. (00:16:33): Maybe a better way to say it is growth mindset, right? You want to look at the possibilities rather than the limitations, and suspend some disbelief and just work on these problems. I just personally feel like I've missed out on more than I've protected myself from. If I sum up both sides of that equation over my career, I wish I had been more open-minded and more optimistic, and more willing to try things, and more focused on possibilities rather than problems. (00:17:00): And so I'm just personally choosing to do that, try to do that as a habit. Nothing deeper than that. I just think it's a better place to be, particularly... It's kind of funny. When I came out here, I was pre-med. I dropped out of school. I came out to be a computer scientist with my friend. I didn't think of it that way. I came out to have a job at Ashton-Tate with a friend of mine, and spent 10 years not understanding that I was actually in a career and thinking that it was a temporary thing where I had to go back to med school and get my degree and be a doctor or something boring like that. And so for 35 years of doing this, it hasn't occurred to me that, oh, actually, I'm in this computer industry that's this technical industry that's constantly growing and constantly inventing things and constantly coming up with these new ideas. And actually, the best posture in that world is to be creative and curious and open and optimistic and try things and stuff like that. (00:17:54): The other thing I'll say about optimism too is related to doing these disruptive things like G Docs. Going back to this idea of all the good ideas look bad at first. Okay, so that's a first principle. That's a sort of fundamental thing of you're going to constantly be challenged by the really good ideas. So how do you overcome it? Well, one way you can overcome it is you want to be able to try things more easily. So part of that is being more optimistic, so being more willing to try stuff, and part of it is also just making it cheaper to try things. (00:18:26): Very early story of G Docs, when I had the idea for Writely, my two co-founders who were both deep domain experts in both app building and word processors were like, "The browser is never going to support this. It's a bad idea. Let's not do this." And they were right and wrong at the same time. They were right that it didn't support even what we have today and wouldn't have supported a full experience, but wrong in that the world was going to change and evolve. And we would never have done the first experiment if it had been a long and costly thing to do, right? (00:18:58): So the fact that our tools were sharp and I could say, "Let's do this thing." And it only takes a couple of days to get it on its feet and see how it feels, it's kind of a form of optimism, right? If you're super pessimistic, you can be like, "Even that's not worth it. Two days is a waste of time." So there's always a little bit of a leap of faith. And then you want to make those as consumable as possible. You want to be able to try things out quickly and learn things and do these experiments. (00:19:23): Now, lots of people have said that before, but I think all those pieces connect for me in this idea of being optimistic and open to trying stuff. Because stuff always is different. You're always wrong about products. That's one of my other rules is you're just always wrong. And so you have to try it. You have to put it in front of people. You have to try it yourself before you'll understand it. No one can really design products in their head completely as far as I can tell.
turns.zh:
挺有趣的，这其实是一种选择。我天生就不是个乐观主义者。真的，我不是。身边所有人，要是听了这番话，只会嘲笑我居然宣扬乐观主义。不过这只是个有意识的选择。悲观主义未必能给你带来什么好处，而粗心大意更是会带来诸多麻烦。你可能会乐观到变得粗心大意，酿成大祸。（00:16:33）或许用“成长型思维模式”来解释更贴切。你要关注可能性而非局限性，暂时放下怀疑，专注于解决问题。回顾我的职业生涯，我觉得自己错失的远比守护住的更多。如果把两边权衡一下，真希望自己能更开明、更乐观，愿意尝试新事物，更多关注可能性而非问题。（00:17:00）所以我选择这样做，把它当作一种习惯。没有更深层的意义。我只是觉得这是一种更好的状态，尤其是……说来挺有趣的。我当初来这儿时，还是个医学预科生。后来退学了，和朋友一起做起了计算机科学家。那时根本没想那么多，只是想在Ashton-Tate找份工作，结果十年过去了，都没意识到自己其实身处这个不断发展、不断创新的技术行业。如今回头看，才发现最该做的，就是保持创造力、好奇心、开放心态，乐观尝试新事物。（00:17:54）关于乐观主义的另一个例子，是G Docs这样的颠覆性项目。回到那个理念：所有好点子一开始看起来都很糟糕。这是个铁律。在好点子面前，你总会面临挑战。如何克服？一种方法是增强尝试的勇气。乐观心态能助你一臂之力，而降低尝试成本同样重要。（00:18:26）G Docs的早期故事：当我提出Writely这个想法时，两位联合创始人——他们都是应用开发和文字处理领域的专家——直言：“浏览器根本不支持这个功能。这是个烂主意，还是别做了。”他们既对又不对。对的是现有技术确实不支持我们今天的成果，更别提完整的用户体验了；错的是世界终将改变进化。如果这是一项漫长而昂贵的实验，我们绝不会迈出第一步。（00:18:58）幸好我们的工具很敏捷，我能说：“就这么干吧。”只需几天就能搭建原型，验证效果。这就是乐观精神的体现。悲观主义者会说：“两天也太浪费时间了。”所以总需要一点信念的飞跃。然后要尽可能降低尝试成本，让创新更易上手。（00:19:23）如今，许多
人们以前也这么说过，但我觉得所有这些因素都指向一个核心理念：保持乐观，勇于尝试新事物。因为世事总是变幻莫测。你对产品的判断往往会出错。这也是我的另一条准则——你永远难免会犯错。所以你必须亲自尝试，把产品呈现给用户。在真正理解它之前，你必须亲自实践。在我看来，没有人能仅凭想象就把产品设计得完美无缺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. There's a few threads I want to follow there. But this is also a tool that I found came up again and again in first-principles thinking, people that are really good at this, is just trying it. There's a lot of just, "Nah, it's not going to work." And exactly as you just described, you often find out you're completely wrong when you actually try it out. And you have this quote, I think in one of your newsletter posts, talking about building Google Docs. You describe it as just fuck around.
turns.zh: 太棒了。那里有几个我感兴趣的帖子。但这个工具在第一性思维中反复出现——那些真正擅长这门技艺的人，就是不断尝试。他们经常会说：“不行，这肯定行不通。” 而正如你刚才描述的，当你真正去尝试时，往往会发现自己大错特错。我记得你在某期通讯中提到过开发Google Docs的经历，你形容那就是“随便试试”。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah. Kind of.
turns.zh: 是啊，有点那个意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Get to the edge of something and fuck around. That's the strategy.
turns.zh: 走到某个边缘，然后随便试试。这就是策略。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Get to the edge is only... Get your tools as sharp as you can get them to be. Make it so that you can try lots of cheap experiments, right? And just mess around and see what happens, see what pops out. And just try to be observant. I think the other part of optimism too is there's a receptiveness to it, right? If you're very pessimistic, you might miss the surprising result that pops out of an experiment. You might force yourself to do a bunch of experiments grudgingly, but you're like, "You know what? I hate this. I'm doing four experiments today because I have to do it because I want to be an entrepreneur, but it sucks and everything's miserable and black." And then you won't notice that, oh, this thing didn't work, but it didn't work in an interesting way. And you're more receptive to that kind of surprising thing, I think, when you're in an optimistic frame of mind. Like, "Oh, let's see how far I can get with this. Oh, it's not working, but why isn't it working? Well, that's kind of interesting. It broke here." (00:21:04): And we've done stuff like that in some of the things, the projects I've got going in Microsoft right now, we've got a chatbot thing we've been working on for a while and with memory, long-running memory so that you can have long conversations with it. And they work okay, but they don't work great in some ways. And we were trying to get multiple versions of them working together, like multi-agents working together. And we gave them whiteboard working memory as a shared working memory thing to fix this problem. And that turns out to make them much smarter. Don't know why. It just makes them smarter. So that was one of these nice little bits of discovery where if you're in a pessimistic frame of mind, you might've said, "Well, these don't work that well, let's give up on it." More optimistic frame of mind was like, "Well, let's try to give them a whiteboard just like a person and see if they cooperate better." And it turns out they really do. So another example of that mindset.
turns.zh: 对。对。走到边缘只是……尽可能磨砺你的工具，让你能进行大量廉价的实验，对吧？然后随便试试，看看会出现什么结果，观察一下。我觉得乐观主义的另一个方面是接受新事物，对吧？如果你太悲观，可能就会错过实验中突如其来的惊喜结果。你可能会不情愿地强迫自己做一堆实验，但你会说：“知道吗？我讨厌这个。我今天因为想当企业家，所以不得不做四个实验，但这太糟糕了，一切都那么黑暗。”然后你就不会注意到，哦，这个没成功，但它以一种有趣的方式失败了。当你处于乐观的心态时，你会更容易注意到这种令人惊喜的结果。比如，“哦，看看我能把这个推多远。哦，它没成功，但为什么没成功呢？嗯，这挺有意思的。它在这里崩掉了。” （00:21:04）：我们在微软的一些项目中也做过类似的事情，比如我们一直在开发的聊天机器人，它有内存功能，可以和用户进行长时间对话。它们还算能用，但在某些方面还不够理想。我们试图让多个版本的聊天机器人协同工作，就像多智能体协同一样。我们给它们白板式的工作记忆作为共享的工作记忆来解决这个问题。这结果发现让它们聪明多了。不知道为什么。就是让它们更聪明了。这就是那种乐观思维的小发现：如果你处于悲观的心态，你可能会说：“嗯，这些效果不太好，还是放弃吧。” 而更乐观的心态则会说：“嗯，让我们给它们一个白板，就像人一样，看看它们能不能更好地合作。” 结果发现它们真的能。所以这就是那种思维模式的又一个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along this thread, I was going to ask about this earlier, but there's a lot of technologies people get optimistic about. Crypto comes to mind, not that there's nothing there, but a lot of people got really optimistic and then it turned out there wasn't really a lot of business to be built and then things entered wintertime. Is there anything you've learned that gives you a signal that, "Lets keep working, I'm going to stay optimistic about this thing?"
turns.zh: 在整个讨论中，我之前想问这个问题，但有很多技术让人乐观。比如加密货币，我不是说它没有前景，但很多人对它太乐观了，结果发现没有太多可发展的商业机会，然后进入寒冬期。你有没有学到什么能给你信号，让你知道“继续努力吧，我对这件事要保持乐观”？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: I spent a lot of time really thinking hard about crypto and whether I was just reacting to it because it threatens some part of my identity or whatever. And I never came down to anything that seemed valuable. I mean, that was always the thing for me is just there has to be a what if that I can say, "Well what if this works? How valuable is it?" And for crypto I was always like, "Well what if it works? Then I have to run up sec on my personal finances. That sounds dystopian. I don't want that." I can't think of anything as a user that I think actually is valuable here, even in the best case. So I feel like the pessimism is justified. (00:22:53): So that's one of my other root principles is just like it's all about user value. Users are lazy, right? We're all lazy. We don't really care that much at the end of the day. No one's going to do something really in their life for any other reason other than it makes their life better. Nobody cares that you're friendly or nice or the logo is pretty or whatever. They care about making their life easier. We're all cynical at heart at some level, so if you can't point at user value, significant user value, it's not going to work. It doesn't matter. Shove all the marketing dollars into it you want, you can write all the articles you want, but it's got to actually solve a problem, a real problem, at the end of the day. I just never saw that with crypto.
turns.zh: 我花了大量时间认真思考加密货币，以及我是否只是因为它威胁到我的某个身份认同或其他因素而对它做出反应。但我始终没有找到任何看似有价值的东西。我的意思是，对我来说，关键在于必须存在一种假设情境——我可以问：“如果它成功了呢？那它会有多大价值？”而对于加密货币，我总是想：“如果它成功了呢？那我就得在个人财务上承受巨大压力。听起来太反乌托邦了。我不想要那样。” 作为用户，我想不出任何真正有价值的东西，即使在最好的情况下也是如此。所以我觉得悲观是合理的。（00:22:53）：所以我的另一个核心原则就是，一切都关乎用户价值。用户是懒惰的，对吧？我们都懒惰。说到底，我们其实并不在乎太多。没有人会为了让生活更美好之外的原因去做任何事。没人会在乎你友好、善良，或者标志设计漂亮之类的。他们只关心让生活更轻松。我们内心深处都有些愤世嫉俗，所以如果你不能指出真正的用户价值，显著的用户价值，那它就不会成功。无论你投入多少营销资金，无论你写多少文章，但最终必须真正解决一个问题，一个切实存在的问题。我在加密货币上从未看到这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I think the lesson there is truly understand if the value is real, versus, this sounds really cool, you think a lot of... Would you want it? I think is a nice exercise there.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我认为这里的教训是，真正理解价值是否真实，而不是“这听起来很酷，你觉得很多人会想要吗？”我觉得这是一个很好的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: We pick on poor Elon, but I feel like with a lot of his products, at least he... He's got lots of other issues, but he articulates clear user value even in the beginning when he's hyping things up. Like Teslas, right? Okay, so electric cars weren't ready, he did the Roadsters, whatever. But he at least articulated this idea that we're going to put a lot of batteries in these things. They're going to really be real cars. They're going to have a real range. We're going to figure out the charging problems. As an end user I'm like, "Okay, that's great. Now I have a car that works like a car that solves some problems that's way cheaper to operate, because the fuel is cheaper. He's solving all the end user problems for me." That at least makes sense. Even if you don't believe that he's going to do it or believe in the way he did it, at least the end user value proposition makes sense, right?
turns.zh: 我们总是嘲笑可怜的埃隆，但我觉得他的很多产品，至少他……他还有很多其他问题，但他至少在一开始宣传产品时就清晰地阐述了用户价值。比如特斯拉，对吧？好吧，当时电动汽车还没准备好，他推出了Roadster之类的。但他至少提出了这样的观点：我们要在这些车里装很多电池。它们会成为真正的汽车。它们会有真正的续航里程。我们会解决充电问题。作为终端用户，我会想：“好吧，很棒。现在我有了一辆能正常运行的车，它解决了一些问题，而且运行成本更低，因为燃油更便宜。他为我解决了所有终端用户的问题。” 这至少是说得通的。即使你不相信他能做到，或者不认同他的做法，但至少终端用户价值主张是合理的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this other great quote in your newsletter, "People are lazy. Look beyond cool too, on how much easier new tool or tech makes someone's life. Convenience always wins." Can you talk about that, just this realization people are just lazy and that's the key?
turns.zh: 你在通讯里还有一句很棒的话：“人们都是懒惰的。除了酷之外，还要看看新工具或新技术能让人们的生活多轻松。便利性总是胜出。” 你能谈谈这句话吗？就是认识到人们就是懒惰，这才是关键？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, well I mean that is the thing. I think as product builders, it's hard to not love what you're doing. You build a product because you love it, you build it because you understand some problem, you build it because you want a paycheck maybe sometimes. But we build it for all these reasons that just do not matter to the end user at all. And if there's one thing I've learned about product, particularly in the consumer space, just kind of in general, is people are just lazy about stuff and don't care about anything other than it making their life better. The thing that's complicated with that is there's two things about it that I think are interesting that follow from that principle. One is, I think products almost follow these thermodynamic rules where if you add a little bit of value, your adoption goes slowly and if you add a lot of value, your adoption goes really quickly, right? (00:25:32): I think ChatGPT is a great recent example of something that was just added a ton of new value to the world and got this explosive growth, and then you see lots of other AI stuff that people are doing that's just not bad, but not great, and it's sort of kind of adding a little bit of value and slowly lumbering along, or maybe it's going to collapse under its weight. That's one thing about the users are lazy part of this. And then the other one I think is, again, it's almost like physics. I think of this as entropy, or people who are confused about entropy or will be like, "Entropy is not real. Look, it runs backwards all the time on earth. Life gets more complicated. What is the deal with entropy?" And like, "Well no, you have to consider the whole system, right? The entire system of the solar system, including the sun is increasing in entropy all the time. We're just making use of some of it." (00:26:24): And I think the same thing is kind of true about user laziness, where people are like, "This tiny thing that I'm focusing on, this feature that I added is better. Therefore, users should adopt it." But you forget all the stuff around it. The user has to hear about it, the user has to remember it in the moment. The user has to learn how to use it, they have to build the habit. That's all effort, right? Not to mention the fact that the actual use of your feature might have friction on the way in, right? It might be hard to sign up for it. (00:26:50): When we did Writely at the beginning, we didn't even ask for an email address, because it was such a novel thing. We didn't want any friction at all in the onboarding process. So you could just come in and make a document and start using it without telling us anything at all about yourself. And after about two minutes of typing, if you're still there, we'd very gently just say, "Please give us your email address, no password, no anything. Just give us your email address so we can send you a URL of this document in case you care about it later. Because if you leave, we'll never know where... We'll never be able to find it again." (00:27:21): But we were super focused on that, as little friction as possible. And I think it's well known in the consumer space, you don't have... The number of seconds you have is not many. 15 seconds, 30 seconds, right, to convince somebody that there's some value there. They're not going to hang out and grind their way through a bunch of high-friction stuff to sign up for your thing. That's the other part of it is just, users will only adopt what you're doing if that sum total of energy that they have to expend is less than the resulting ease in their life that they get, usually by a factor of at least a couple, right? So it has to make your life a lot better, hopefully a really a lot better, like 10X better than what you spend to use it.
turns.zh:
是啊，我是说，这就是关键所在。我认为作为产品开发者，很难不热爱自己正在做的事情。你开发一款产品是因为热爱它，开发它是因为理解某个问题，开发它可能有时只是为了拿薪水。但我们开发产品的所有这些原因，对终端用户来说其实都无关紧要。如果说我对产品有所领悟，尤其是在消费领域，总体来说就是人们对事物很懒散，除了能让生活更美好之外，对其他任何东西都不在乎。复杂之处在于，基于这个原则，有两个有趣的现象。首先，我认为产品几乎遵循热力学法则——如果你增加一点价值，用户采用速度会很慢；如果你增加大量价值，用户采用速度会非常快，对吧？（00:25:32）我认为ChatGPT就是最近一个很好的例子，它为世界增添了大量新价值，获得了爆炸式增长。而你会看到很多其他AI产品，虽然也不差，但不够出色，只是增加了一点价值，发展缓慢，甚至可能因自身重量而崩塌。这就是用户懒散的另一方面。然后，另一个让我感兴趣的点是，这几乎像物理学。我把这看作熵。或者对熵感到困惑的人可能会问：“熵不是真实存在的。看地球上熵一直在倒退。生活变得越来越复杂。熵到底怎么回事？”而我的回答是：“不，你必须考虑整个系统，对吧？包括太阳在内的整个太阳系的熵一直在增加。我们只是在利用其中一部分。”（00:26:24）关于用户懒散，我认为同样适用熵的原理。人们会说：“我专注的这个小功能，添加的这个特性更好。因此，用户应该采用它。”但你忽略了周围的一切。用户必须听说过它，必须在当下记住它。用户必须学会如何使用它，必须养成习惯。这都是努力，对吧？更不用说实际使用你的功能可能会遇到摩擦，比如注册困难。（00:26:50）我们最初做Writely时，甚至不要求用户提供邮箱地址，因为这太新奇了。我们不想在入门流程中增加任何摩擦。所以你可以直接进来创建文档并开始使用，而无需告诉我们任何个人信息。大约两分钟的输入后，如果你还在，就温和地提示：“请给我们你的邮箱地址，不需要密码，只需邮箱地址，这样我们就能把文档的URL发送给你，以防你之后需要用到它。如果你离开，我们就再也找不到它了……” （00:27:21）但我们非常专注于尽可能减少摩擦。在消费领域众所周知的是，你没有太多时间——15秒、30秒——来说服别人产品有价值。他们不会为了注册你的产品而费力克服高摩擦的障碍。这就是另一个关键点：只有当用户为采用你的产品所需耗费的总能量小于产品为他们生活带来的便利时，他们才会采用你的产品。
通常来说，回报率至少要翻几倍，对吧？所以它必须能让你的生活大大改善，最好是那种显著的改善——比如比你使用它的花费高出十倍的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I think of as you're describing this is, Microsoft Excel had a billion toolbars and buttons and options, which allowed Google Docs essentially to come in with a much simpler experience. Now you're on the other side of that, which is I didn't think about.
turns.zh: 听你描述这件事时，我想到的是微软Excel当时有无数的工具栏、按钮和选项，这让Google Docs得以推出一个更加简洁的界面。现在我们却反其道而行之，这点我之前完全没想到。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, it's a really funny place to be. And it's funny to be at Microsoft, because I'm kind of the enemy, right? Because I'm the guy who messed them up a little bit. So there's some friction around that. Yeah, I mean I think there are similar trade-offs to be made right now, by the way, with AI. I think there's similar opportunities. But we made this choice with... So it's a little hard to remember, right? Because it's like 18 years, 17 years ago now, 18 years ago almost. In that era, Office was impregnable, right? So software had to be distributed physically, right, it had to be shipped around, it had to be bought and installed. It was harder to use. (00:29:01): And so there's a very high transactional cost. Because there's a very high transactional cost, the buyers would always make this decision like, "Do I want the thing with 1,000 features or the thing with 995 features? I don't know what those last five are, but I might as well have all of them." And so that was just the lock-in for Microsoft, right? So we made this trade-off, we're like, "Look, we're easy to use, we're zero install, you don't have to ever deal with it, it's super convenient. Plus you get this one new feature that's really, really useful, which is collaborating with each other and not having to send attachments around the old file servers, but we're going to take away most of the features, because we don't care about them that much." (00:29:39): And we took away a little bit more than we should have. In the early days, we'd get all these complaints about people who wanted word count, which I thought was a really weird... I thought that was going to be way at the end of the list. We didn't have rulers, we didn't have any kind of formatting at that point, any real pagination. We just had these basic documents. But page word count came in, of course it was students, was one of our early adopters. So they really wanted to know if they were at the word count for the essay that they had just had assigned to them. (00:30:06): So there was this dance with Microsoft that we deliberately made this trade-off. And I think it's almost like a classic innovator's dilemma model, right? We had this incumbent that was asymptotically approaching usefulness, they're adding stuff. Whenever they added stuff, it wasn't really that much more valuable. And then we were this small thing that came in into a market that they didn't care that much about, that they didn't understand that well, which is the internet stuff, this disruptive new thing. We just chipped away from the bottom, like the innovator's dilemma. And I think it was hard for Microsoft to respond to it. I think it took them a while to even have a clear idea of how they were going to respond to it. In retrospect, they did fine. We took a bunch of market share, but they kept all the money basically. So we being Google. So they survived it. They did a good job surviving the challenge. We have all the users now, but they have all the money. We have all the money, I guess now.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个很有趣的处境。在微软工作也很有意思，因为我算是个"敌人"，对吧？毕竟我曾让他们吃过不少苦头。所以这中间存在着不少摩擦。说到AI，现在我们也面临着类似的权衡。机会是相似的，但我们当时做出了不同的选择。说起来有点难记了，毕竟已经过去18年、17年、快18年了。那个时代，Office简直坚不可摧，对吧？软件必须实体分发、安装、购买，使用体验很糟糕。（00:29:01）交易成本极高，所以用户总会纠结："是选择有1000项功能的产品，还是995项功能的？我不知道那最后五项是什么，但还是全要了吧"。这就是微软的锁定效应。我们权衡后决定："我们要简单易用，无需安装，随用随用，超级方便。再加上一个真正有用的功能——协作无需通过旧的文件服务器发送附件。"但我们去掉了太多功能，本该保留更多的。早期用户抱怨缺少字数统计，我觉得这很奇怪...我以为这功能会排在需求列表的末尾。我们那时没有标尺、格式设置、分页功能，只有最基本的文档。但用户确实需要字数统计，尤其是学生群体，他们想知道论文字数是否达标。（00:30:06）我们故意和微软博弈，权衡利弊。这几乎是经典的创新者困境模式：现有巨头功能逐渐完善，但增量价值有限；我们则像创新者一样，逐步蚕食市场份额。这就是创新者困境。微软很难应对挑战，花了很久才找到应对策略。回头看，他们处理得不错。我们抢占了市场份额，但微软基本保住了利润。所以我们成了Google。他们成功渡过了难关，现在我们用户多，但钱还是他们赚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to spend more time on Google Docs and the story there. A couple questions. How long did it take from starting on it to feeling like it's working? Whatever you consider product market fit.
turns.zh: 我想多花些时间在Google Docs上，并深入探讨其背后的故事。请问几个问题：从开始着手到感觉它真正运转起来，这整个过程花了多长时间？还有，您如何定义产品与市场的契合度？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Almost immediately, honestly. It was weird, the process of it was, I had this idea, we set this thing up, we started working together. We're like, "Ah, that's actually pretty..." So basically history is like I noticed contents editable, so the browser would do some editing for you. And then I noticed JavaScript, I never realized that JavaScript is out there. And we had done word processors in the past, this team, and for a long time. In fact, my co-founder, Steve, the other person on that document, wrote this thing called Full Write way back in 1987 or something like that, that was a direct competitor. '85 I think even, that was a direct competitor to Word one. (00:31:57): So we knew word processors, and so we decided to just try it. What's it like to build a word processor? And the fact that you could collaborate on them was kind of an accident. They're just these things on the server. We hadn't built the thing that would lock somebody out yet. So there was just like, "Here's a document, you can edit these two things." Which we, A, immediately realized was really cool. We could both work in the same document at the same time. And then, B, realized, "Oh, crap, we're colliding with each other, because there's no presence or anything like that. And there's no collision detection or anything like that." (00:32:26): So pretty quickly we're like, "Oh, that's kind of cool. That feels good as a development team to have these shared documents, not to send stuff around and not... So that's cool. So let's build that out." But like, "Oh, bummer, collaboration's a problem. We'll have to go fix that." And naively figured out that that's a problem. And it took forever to get that working. It was really, really hard in the time, because we didn't do operational transform. I don't think that technique had been quite invented yet. And so we did three-way merge, which doesn't work that well, because the browsers... The logical document, a document can be rendered differently in HTML. There's not a canonical representation. (00:33:04): And so you're doing merges where alphabetization can change, the order of attributes can change, the tree structure can change. Firefox would do a blank paragraph with a singleton BR tag, and IE would do it with an open closed paragraph tag. And so even the tree doesn't match. So it's a really hard merge problem. So that turned out to be a gnarly hard problem to solve. But once we had seen the value of working together, we were motivated to do that. (00:33:32): The interesting thing too with that is, I think if we'd gotten it in the other order, we might not have done it. It's another good example of why not and what if, right? Where we got really lucky that we saw the what if part, that we saw how cool a document in a browser that you could collaborate on would be, because if we understood how hard the collaboration piece would've been first without understanding that value, we might've been like, "Eh, it's not worth it. It's going to be so hard to solve that problem. It's probably not a useful app." So I think it's a good little counter example of that optimistic, pessimistic perspective we were talking about. We could easily have missed that idea, easily have missed that idea. And we just got lucky I think in the order it got presented to us.
turns.zh:
老实说，几乎是立刻就决定了。整个过程很奇怪——我突然有了这个想法，我们搭建起框架，开始合作。我们当时就感叹：“哇，这其实挺酷的……” 基本上，历史是这样的，我注意到了“内容可编辑”功能，这样浏览器就能帮你进行编辑。然后我发现了JavaScript，从来不知道还有JavaScript这种技术。我们团队过去长期做过文字处理软件。事实上，我的联合创始人史蒂夫（Steve）在1987年左右写过一个叫Full Write的直接竞争产品。我记得1985年左右，我们的产品甚至直接对标了微软的Word。

（00:31:57）：所以我们熟悉文字处理软件，就决定试试看。开发文字处理软件到底是什么感觉？最初实现协作功能纯属意外。那些文档只是存放在服务器上的，当时我们还没开发出锁定功能。所以只能这样：“这里有个文档，你可以编辑这两个地方。” 结果我们发现，A，立刻意识到这很酷。能同时在同一文档上协作真是太棒了。B，接着发现：“糟糕，我们互相冲突了，因为没有状态管理之类的东西，也没有冲突检测机制。” （00:32:26）：很快我们就说：“嗯，这挺酷的。作为开发团队，能共享文档而不用到处发送文件，感觉很棒。所以就继续开发吧。” 但接着发现：“唉，协作真是个难题。我们得去修复它。” 天真地以为这只是个技术问题。结果花了很久才搞定。当时技术难度很大，因为我们没有做操作转换技术。当时这项技术还没完全发明出来。所以我们用了三向合并，但效果不理想，因为浏览器对同一文档的呈现方式不同，没有统一的标准格式。

（00:33:04）：合并时字母顺序可能变，属性顺序可能乱，树结构可能错。火狐会用空白段落和单个BR标签，IE则用开放闭合的段落标签。连树结构都不一致。这是个极难解决的合并问题。好在我们看到了协作的价值，才有动力继续下去。

（00:33:32）：有趣的是，如果当时顺序反过来，我们可能就放弃了。这又是一个“如果……会怎样”的好例子。如果我们先理解协作有多难，再看到协作的价值，可能就放弃了。所以这又是一个很好的例子，说明我们之前讨论的乐观与悲观视角。当时我们很容易错过这个想法，真是运气好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting actually, that you need to be pulled to the what if getting you so excited that you're going to spend however many years it took you to solve that problem, because you are so excited about this what if. I think that's a really good-
turns.zh: 实际上这真的很有趣，你需要被某个假设所吸引，兴奋到愿意花费多年时间去解决这个问题，就因为你对这个假设充满热情。我觉得这真的很棒——

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, I mean I've spent a lot of time. It's kind of funny, I keep expecting people to just be like, "All right, grandpa, stop talking about G Docs. It's been a long time." Right? So it has been a long time. It's been 17 years, but it's still very relevant. It's got a couple billion users now I think, it's a big thing. But I've spent a lot of the last 10 or 15 years just thinking about, why did that work? What worked about that? What lessons can I draw from it? There was a lot of energy around it, positive and negative. The first week I was at Google, an executive there refused to give me hardware, because he thought that Google was an app company not a... It was a search company, not an app company. And literally the guy in charge of hardware at the time refused to give me hardware for this service. And I had to threaten to either sue him or haul him in front of Eric Schmidt, because I had a contract and I had contracted earnouts. (00:35:20): So that was another one of these interesting lessons of sometimes the opposition is enormous. And if I had just been a random Google employee with this idea and no legal protection, and the CEO wasn't a fan of the project, it would've died. There's no way it would've made it through that negativity and that pessimism and that person being either challenged or afraid of the idea, or just not able to imagine it, or what. I'm not sure what. But we'll keep coming back to this idea of optimism, but I have this very strong feeling about that most of the reason people don't do really innovative good products is this kind of mindset. You're just not seeing the opportunities. (00:36:02): There's a lot of hard work for sure. There's a lot of stuff that you can read about and best practices of doing iteration and user testing and user interviews and really listening and all the engineering best practices. That stuff is pretty mechanical. Once you know where you're going, you can do that. It's not that hard to learn and to master it. I think the hard stuff is this mindset of being open in the right ways and understanding that some kinds of pushback are good pushback. Some are bad. (00:36:32): I always think that product builders and entrepreneurs, you have this really hard problem of you have to be very rigid about your mission. I know where I'm going. I know what my mission is, and I'm going to go there because the world doesn't care, it's going to push back. But you also have to be really flexible about feedback. You're probably aren't going to be right about a bunch of it. And so you have to blend these two things together somehow. It's like a samurai sword that's hard on the back, but softer on the edge so it doesn't break. Or the other way around I think. But there's this hard thing you have to do as an entrepreneur, and I think it's the real core of building really great products is finding that balance and really listening to those signals, being open to it.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，我确实花了不少时间。说起来挺有趣的，我总期待别人会说：“好吧，老兄，别再谈G Docs了，都过去17年了。”对吧？确实已经过去17年了，但它至今仍具现实意义。现在用户数量估计有几十亿了，这是个大项目。但过去10到15年里，我大部分时间都在思考：为什么那个方案能成功？成功的关键是什么？能从中吸取哪些经验教训？当时围绕它有各种各样的声音，有正面的也有负面的。我到谷歌的第一周，就有个高管拒绝给我硬件设备，因为他觉得谷歌是应用公司，不是……他认为谷歌是搜索公司，不是应用公司。当时负责硬件的负责人甚至拒绝为这个服务提供硬件。我不得不威胁要起诉他，或者把他带到埃里克·施密特面前，因为我签了合同，还有赚取分成条款。（00:35:20）这又是一个有趣的教训：有时候反对的声音会非常强烈。如果我只是个普通的谷歌员工，没有法律保护，CEO又不喜欢这个项目，那这个项目肯定夭折了。根本不可能突破那些负面情绪、悲观看法，以及对这个想法持质疑、恐惧或无法想象的人的阻力。我不确定具体原因。但我们会不断回归到乐观主义这个主题，但我深信，大多数人之所以做不出真正创新的好产品，往往源于这种思维模式。你就是看不到机会。（00:36:02）当然需要付出大量努力。你可以阅读很多关于迭代、用户测试、用户访谈的最佳实践指南，认真倾听用户反馈，掌握所有工程最佳实践。这些东西比较机械。一旦你明确了方向，就能做到这些。学习和掌握这些技能并不难。我认为困难之处在于以正确的方式保持开放心态，理解某些反对意见是良性的，有些则是恶意的。（00:36:32）我一直认为产品开发者和创业者面临着一个非常艰难的挑战：你必须对自己的使命坚定不移。我知道自己的目标，我知道自己的使命所在，我会朝着目标前进，因为世界不会在意，世界会不断反抗。但你又必须对反馈保持灵活。你对很多反馈的判断很可能不正确。所以你必须找到某种平衡方式。这就像一把武士剑，背面很硬，但刀锋很柔软，这样它才不会折断。我觉得应该是反过来。但作为创业者，你必须面对这个难题，我认为打造真正伟大产品的核心在于找到这种平衡，真正倾听那些信号，保持开放心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also knowing how long to commit to it versus time to move on to something else. So along those lines, what was the moment where you finally felt product market fit for what became Google Docs, and how long was that from the beginning of starting to work on it?
turns.zh: 还要知道应该投入多少时间来专注于它，以及何时该转向其他项目。说到这儿，您是何时最终认定Google Docs产品与市场契合的？从开始着手开发到实现这一目标，整个过程耗时多久？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: It depends on what market we're talking about. I've been continually surprised at the adoption of G Docs. I think we knew there was something there pretty quickly, probably in the first couple months. There was a lot of energy around it. It was a weird ride, because we built this thing on a whim, and as an experiment. We liked it. We decided to go just advertise on Google. At the time, 37signals was the cool company. And we're like, "That looks cool. We'll just be some engineers and we'll have a little subscription SaaS business thing and chill out. So let's see what it costs to acquire customers. So let's go advertise on Google and see how much it costs to get people to sort of show up, and then we'll figure out if we have a subscription business or not." (00:38:12): And that just got us noticed. That got us noticed by Google. It got us noticed. We were I think one of the first 10 articles at TechCrunch, like Michael Arrington. Another funny story is that I had a breakfast with Michael Arrington at Bucks, in that era where he was trying to decide, he had this spreadsheet idea he wanted to work on and he was trying to decide he should go do that and maybe join forces with us, because we were cool, or if he should continue to work on this blog thing he had gone called TechCrunch. So I might be partially responsible for TechCrunch, because we turned him down and said, "You should go do TechCrunch instead." Every time I would bump into him, I would laugh about that one. (00:38:50): But when we got noticed, we really got noticed. There was just this period where we were the hot thing for a couple months, where every VC wanted to talk to us and everyone's trying to figure it out. Because I think we're like... When you see one point on the line, like Gmail, which came before us, you're like, "Oh, that's kind of cool. That's an interesting quasi-app." But it's like a weird kind of app. It's serialized. You can't really interact with it that much. And then you see this as another point on the curve and you're like, "Oh, that's a real app. Oh, crap. I wonder, is there anything stopping us from doing the rest of Office? Oh, probably not. How far is this going to go?" (00:39:27): And so I think we were that second point that showed that there was actually this totally different paradigm. And so we just got this enormous amount of tension pretty quickly. And then the rest of it was feeling our way through what does it actually mean? How much of the functionality do we need to build? What's the really important part about it? How much of its collaboration? We spent a bunch of energy on offline, which was miserable, which never turned out to matter that much. (00:39:51): Now that team has spent a long time replicating all these features that we abandoned by the wayside, which I think I'm not that interested in. I think the future of documents looks very different than what we have now. I think it's kind of funny now that we're spending billions of dollars on GPUs to emulate wind pulp and ink pressed by metal type. We're building linear documents that are fixed, that are static. So one of the things we've been doing with these chatbot things is they also serve as documents. I say bots or docs all the time. And so you'll do these things where you... I do this all the time, where we'll interview... We'll create a new one. It has a separate identity, as a separate document, and then you tell it like, "I'm going to write a technical document. Here's roughly what it's about. Why don't you interview me?" (00:40:35): So it interviews you for an hour, and now you've got this nice linear artifact which you can read. It's very readable because it's conversational. But at the same time, you've been building all these semantically encoded virtual synthetic memories in the Spectre database. So you can come in and say, "Show me a diagram of this. Draw this diagram for me, change it in the following way. What is this? If I change this, what if I change that? Summarize this part of it." So you can start to interact with it. That's still creating stuff at the bottom of this linear artifact. But the next step that we're working on now is just making that dynamic where you just come to something and you talk to it and interact with it. (00:41:12): I think one of the things that's going to happen is, just like it seems... Well, in the early days of G Docs, people would say, "Well, what if I'm not connected?" And one of the things I would say is, "In three or five years, if you get handed a device that's not connected to the internet, your word for it is going to be broken." Which is true, right? It's anachronistic and weird if something's not connected. I think we're going to feel the same way about intention and interactivity in our products very soon. If I can't tell something what my intent is and have it configure itself in an intelligent way, have it converse with me, whether that's a device or a piece of GUI UX somewhere, I think it's going to feel anachronistic. It's going to feel really weird. (00:41:55): There's that scene in one of the early Star Trek movies where Scotty tries to talk to the mouse, right? He's like, "Computer make the..." He's pissed off because he can't talk to the computer. We're all going to be like that in five years I think, about it. And it's going to seem really weird that we have these applications that I can't collaborate with the application. Why can't I collaborate with the applications? It's like the application's locked on a file server just like the pre G Docs days. Why can't I just interact with it and have it configure itself the way I want it to configure itself, and show me the data the way I want to see this, and let me build the workflow the way I want it, and remember it for me and bring it back later, and all that stuff? So that was a long digression, but I would just like... You're asking about features and functionality, and I feel like where we are now with these feature wars, it's just silly. It's not the point at all. I think documents are going to change radically in the next few years.
turns.zh:
这取决于我们所谈论的市场。我对G Docs的普及速度一直感到惊讶。我认为我们很早就意识到这个产品有潜力，可能是在最初的几个月里。当时大家对它充满热情。这是一段奇特的历程——我们一时兴起开发了这个产品，当作一个实验项目。我们喜欢它，就决定在谷歌上投放广告。当时37signals可是很酷的公司。我们心想：“这看起来很棒。我们就当几个工程师，搞个订阅式SaaS业务，放松一下。先看看获取客户的成本是多少，再决定是否要发展订阅业务。” （00:38:12）结果这让我们受到了关注。谷歌注意到了我们。每次我们在TechCrunch上被提及时，比如Michael Arrington的报道，我都会想起这段趣事。（00:38:50）但当我们真正受到关注时，那段热度确实持续了几个月。每个风投都想和我们聊天，大家都在研究这个模式。因为我们就像……当你看到Gmail这样的前例时，你会觉得：“哦，那挺酷的，是个有趣的准应用。”但它更像个奇怪的应用，序列化存储，互动性不强。再看看G Docs，你会意识到这才是真正的应用。天啊，我们能不能把Office剩下的功能都实现了？应该可以吧。它能走多远呢？ （00:39:27）所以我认为我们是第二个证明存在全新范式的存在。随后我们迅速面临巨大压力。接下来要考虑的是：我们需要构建哪些功能？最核心的部分是什么？协作功能有多重要？我们在离线功能上投入了大量精力，但结果并不理想。（00:39:51）现在团队花了很长时间重现那些被我们抛弃的功能，我对此并不感兴趣。我认为文档的未来会与现在截然不同。现在我们花数十亿美元在GPU上模拟金属活字排版的纸质文档，真是讽刺。我们构建的是固定、静态的线性文档。我们在聊天机器人上的尝试也表明，它们同样可以作为文档。我总是不停地说“机器人”或“文档”。比如采访新嘉宾时，我们会创建一个独立的文档，然后告诉它：“我要写一份技术文档，大概内容是这样的，你来采访我吧。” （00:40:35）于是它会采访你一个小时，最后形成一份完整的文档。
如今，你得到了这份易于阅读的线性艺术品——它之所以读起来顺畅，是因为采用了口语化的表达方式。但与此同时，你一直在Spectre数据库中构建大量语义编码的虚拟合成记忆。因此，你可以进入系统并说：“给我展示这部分图表。帮我画出这个图表，并按照以下方式修改它。这是什么？如果我更改这个部分，又会如何影响那个部分？请总结这部分内容。”这样你就能开始与系统进行交互。这仍是在线性艺术品底层进行的创造性工作。然而，我们目前正在努力实现的下一步，是让这种交互变得动态化——你只需走到某个界面前，与它对话并进行互动。（00:41:12）：我认为未来会出现这样的情况，就像……嗯，在G Docs早期阶段，人们会问：“如果我无法联网会怎样？”而我当时会回应：“三到五年后，如果你拿到一台无法联网的设备，你的第一反应肯定是‘这设备太落伍了’。”确实如此，对吧？当某个设备无法联网时，我们会觉得它过时且怪异。我觉得很快我们也会对产品中的意图与交互性产生同样的感受。如果我无法告知某个设备我的意图，而它又无法智能配置自身、与我对话——无论是设备还是某个图形用户界面（GUI）——我觉得这也会让人觉得过时和怪异。（00:41:55）：在《星际迷航》早期电影中有个场景，斯科蒂试图与鼠标对话，对吧？他大喊：“电脑，执行……” 他因为无法与电脑交流而愤怒。我觉得五年后我们大家都会有同样的体验。当面对无法与应用程序协作的应用时，我们会感到困惑——为什么我不能与应用程序互动，让它按照我的需求配置自身，按照我希望的方式展示数据，构建我想要的工作流，并为我保存并调用这些数据？这真是个长篇大论，但我只是想……你问的是功能和特性，而我觉得我们现在卷入的这场功能竞赛实在太荒谬了。这根本不是重点。我认为未来几年文档会发生根本性的变革。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow that thread. Before I do, I found the first TechCrunch post about you guys. Starts with, "Imagine Word, but as an Ajax browser application."
turns.zh: 我想跟进一下那个话题。在开始之前，我发现了TechCrunch上关于你们团队的第一篇报道："想象一下，Word如果是一个Ajax浏览器应用会是什么样子。"

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Oh, yeah, there you go. Yeah. It wasn't even JavaScript. It was Ajax.
turns.zh: 哦，对，就是这样。当时甚至都不是JavaScript，而是Ajax。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ajax, so hot back then.
turns.zh: Ajax，那时候可是个热门话题。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: It's also funny too, because I'll talk to young front end developers these days. I'm like, "I don't want to scare you too much, but jQuery didn't even exist when I wrote this thing. This is like bare metal in the DOM, and there were bugs." When I went to Google, I had to write this little network stack at the bottom of the JavaScript that in theory [inaudible 00:43:21] you could interrupt, you could have multiple requests inflate and you can interrupt them and discard them and stuff. (00:43:25): But the stack at the time was really buggy, and I think it was IEE. And so I wrote this little network queue that would keep track of whether there were requests in flight, and kill them in a way that didn't break everything. And it was hard to do, because it's this weird asynchronous programming. And that piece of code, when I went to Google, they made me reformat it for the JavaScript readability standards, and I could not get it to work with their formatting. There was some bug in the JavaScript compiler of the time that whitespace mattered. And so I wound up checking it in broken, got the readability badge and immediately fixed it. It's like that was another one of our little hacks to get this working.
turns.zh: 说起来挺有趣的，因为现在我会和年轻的前端开发者聊天，说"我不想吓到你们，但我写这段代码的时候jQuery还没问世呢。这就像是直接操作DOM的原始层，还到处都是bug。"去谷歌工作时，我不得不在JavaScript底层写一个小网络栈，理论上[00:43:21未录音]你可以中断请求、并发多个请求并取消它们之类的。但当时的栈漏洞百出，应该是IE的问题。所以我写了一个小网络队列，用来跟踪正在进行的请求，并以不影响整体运行的方式终止它们。这很难实现，因为这是种奇怪的异步编程。结果谷歌的代码格式化工具把我的代码格式改得乱七八糟，我怎么都调不正常。当时的JavaScript编译器有白空符问题，这导致代码无法正常运行。最后我只能提交一个残缺的版本，贴上可读性警告标签，立刻修复了问题。那也是我们为了让项目成功而做的又一个小技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. This episode is brought to you by Ahrefs. Many of you already know Ahrefs as one of the top tools for search engine optimization. It's used by thousands of SEOs and companies like IBM, Adidas, and eBay. What you may not know is that there's a free version that was made with small website owners in mind. It's called Ahrefs Webmaster Tools. It's free and it can help you bring more traffic to your website. Ahrefs Webmaster Tools will show you keywords that you rank for and back links that you can get. It also performs automated site audits to find what issues prevent your website from ranking higher on Google. Every detected issue comes with a detailed explanation and advice on how to fix it. Visit ahrefs.com/AWT, set up a free account, connect your website and start improving it. That's A-H-R-E-F-S dot com/AWT. (00:44:58): There's often this criticism as an engineer, you just want to work on interesting things and work on the technology before you find a problem that it's solving. It feels like with this example it was, you just think this is a cool technology, let's see what happens. Do you have any, I don't know, learnings or advice for when it's actually fine. Let's just play with this tech, be at the edges, you said, and maybe it'll lead somewhere, versus you should probably try to avoid that and first focus on a problem.
turns.zh:
我太喜欢这个话题了。本期节目由Ahrefs赞助。很多人都知道Ahrefs是搜索引擎优化的顶级工具之一，数千名SEO专家和IBM、阿迪达斯、eBay等公司都在用它。但你可能不知道，Ahrefs还有一个免费版，专为小型网站所有者设计。它叫Ahrefs Webmaster Tools，免费使用，能帮你提升网站流量。Ahrefs Webmaster Tools会展示你排名的关键词和能获取的反向链接，还能自动审核网站，找出阻碍网站在谷歌上获得更高排名的问题。每个检测到的问题都会附带详细解释和修复建议。访问ahrefs.com/AWT，注册免费账户，连接你的网站并开始优化。就是A-H-R-E-F-S点com/AWT。
(00:44:58): 作为工程师，经常有人批评你只想做有趣的事，先钻研技术再去解决问题。比如这个例子，你可能就是觉得这项技术很酷，先看看会发生什么。关于何时可以这样做，你有什么建议吗？就是放手去玩新技术，站在前沿，也许会有收获，但你应该避免这样做，先专注于解决问题。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: I'm guilty of that. I mean, I like to play with stuff. I tend to think with my fingers as much as anything else. So I actually think there's a good place for just play with the tech a lot and figure out what it's good for. What I've evolved to doing these days with my teams is I pick what I call north stars that I think are interesting, useful things to get to rather than just messing around. What's a cool thing that I think might be buildable with this? (00:45:49): So right now we're doing these multi-agent systems. We're trying to figure out how much independent work they can do without a person holding their hand. And so a nice domain to test that out in is programming, because you don't have a whole lot of... You just give something a Python environment and a file system and that's it and that's all it needs. And so you're not distracted by connectivity issues or whatever. (00:46:11): So one of the problems right now is go write the eye in Python. That's a problem I could give to an intern and it would take them a summer to do some halfway decent job of it. It's a thing you could expect a reasonably competent programmer to do, mostly independently. And so it should be possible for the system, if it's independent at all, to go do that. So is that useful by itself? No, because we already have the eye, it doesn't matter. But if we build a system of programming agents that can self-monitor and self-correct and bug themselves, that can build things that are roughly that scale of complexity, that's valuable. That would be a valuable thing to have. (00:46:43): It's kind of interesting too, because that system already, it's produced a bunch of good insights. One of them is its kind of complicated and then hard to debug it. It's this asynchronous system of stochastic agents. That's a lot of stuff to deal with. So we wrote a debugger agent. And debugger agent watches stuff, and when there's a problem somewhere, it goes and figures out what the problem is and then gives you a nice explanation of what you broke and what needs to be fixed. And we haven't turned it loose on actually fixing things yet because we don't trust it, but it's very helpful as an assistant [inaudible 00:47:15]. We had one that documented itself too. That's the other one we did recently. Just turned it loose on documenting the code base and did a pretty good job of it. (00:47:21): So it's starting to produce interesting stuff, right? Because we have these north stars that we aim things at. And I think that's maybe a good antidote to this. Just playing with tech without being focused doesn't tend to produce anything that's super valuable. But picking these, even if they're arbitrary goals, as long as they're real goals that you're trying to get to, that's useful, right? Where you're like, "I wonder if I can get this to work. I wonder if I can build this thing." Then grind away at that for a week and see how close I can get. See what I learned about why it's hard. That's probably better than just like, "Let me poke at JavaScript for a while."
turns.zh: 我也深有同感。我是说，我喜欢摆弄各种东西。我倾向于用手指来思考问题。所以我认为，有时候多花时间玩转技术，探索它的潜力，是很有意义的。如今我和团队一起做的事情，是挑选一些我称之为"北极星"的项目——那些我认为值得探索、实用的东西，而不是漫无目的地折腾。（00:45:49）比如说，我们现在正在研究多智能体系统。我们试图弄清楚，在没有人工干预的情况下，它们能完成多少独立工作。编程领域是个测试这种能力的好领域，因为你不需要太多额外条件——只需给它们一个Python环境和文件系统，就能让它们运作起来，不受其他因素干扰。（00:46:11）当前的一个难题是用Python编写眼睛模块。这项任务我可以交给实习生，让他们花一个夏天完成一个还算不错的版本。但对于一个能力一般的程序员来说，独立完成这项任务应该不难。所以如果系统真的能独立运作，就应该能够完成这个任务。那么这项任务本身有用吗？不算，因为我们已经有了现成的眼睛模块，所以这没什么意义。但如果我们能构建一个能够自我监控、自我纠错、自我调试的编程智能体系统，能够构建出大致相同复杂度的应用，那才是有价值的。（00:46:43）这项系统已经产生了很多有益的见解。比如，它的异步随机智能体系统非常复杂，调试起来很困难。为此我们开发了一个调试器智能体。调试器会监控系统，当出现问题时，它会分析问题原因，并给出清晰的修复建议。虽然我们还没让它真正去修复问题，因为我们还不信任它，但它作为助手已经非常有用了。（00:47:21）所以它开始产出有趣的成果了，对吧？因为我们有这些明确的目标——北极星。我觉得这或许是克服浮躁的良药。漫无目的地摆弄技术往往无法产出真正有价值的东西。但即使这些目标是随意设定的，只要它们是真实的目标，那就是有意义的，对吧？比如你会想，"我能让这个东西运行起来吗？我能构建这个东西吗？"然后花一周时间埋头攻克，观察能达到怎样的程度。看看自己为什么会遇到困难。这比随便玩玩JavaScript要强多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's also different, I think, at a bigger company where you need to achieve something, versus I think as just an engineer out of college just playing around, like, go for it, right? It's just like, what's the worst that could happen?
turns.zh: 我觉得在大公司里，需要达成目标和作为刚毕业的工程师随意摆弄技术的情况也不同。大公司里你必须有所成就，而刚毕业的工程师可能只想随心所欲地折腾。就像，“最坏能怎样呢？”

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Even the early days of Writely, the very... I mean, we had a goal from the beginning. The beginning was like, "Can I write a word processor in a browser?" That was literally the problem statement, right? It was like, "I have content edible, I have Ajax or JavaScript. Can I put these together and something that feels like a word processor? Let's go do that." It's kind of half messing around with tech, but it's also half an actual goal. So I don't know. (00:48:35): I like playing around with... I think a lot of the good product ideas, most of the good product ideas actually come up from engineering. So I think there's a lot to be said for, get familiar with tools, particularly weird esoteric combinations of tools can often be useful. If you understand or three things... At Google, I was one of only two people in the company who had the code readability, which is the right to check in code in this language, and both a backend language, which is the monitoring language, Org Mode, a middle tier language, which is Java, and a front language, which is JavaScript. No one else would do that full stack. I think it's useful to have that broad perspective sometimes.
turns.zh: 即使是 Writely 的早期阶段，嗯……我是说，我们从一开始就有一个目标。最初的想法是：“我能在浏览器里开发一个文字处理器吗？”这就是问题的核心，对吧？当时我们是：“我有可编辑的内容，有 Ajax 或 JavaScript。能把它们整合起来，做出一个类似文字处理器的东西吗？那就动手做吧。”这既有点技术探索的意味，也确实是个明确的目标。说起来也挺有趣的。（00:48:35）：我喜欢折腾……我觉得很多优秀的产品创意，大多数好点子其实都源自工程实践。所以我认为，多熟悉各种工具很重要，尤其是那些看似奇特的工具组合往往能派上用场。比如你要理解三种语言：在 Google 时，我是公司里仅有的两个拥有代码可读性权限的人之一——既能用 Java 写后端代码，又能用 Org Mode 处理中间层，还能用 JavaScript 写前端代码。没人能全栈掌握这些技术。有时拥有广阔的视野确实很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sam, the Renaissance man of all languages.
turns.zh: 山姆，真是个语言全才。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: Yeah, ADD more like it, but yeah, I pay attention to things.
turns.zh: 是啊，多些这样的想法，不过我确实会留意这些细节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wanted to follow this thread a little further around being good at these what if questions. It feels like you've built this, or maybe you were born with this skill of thinking in the future, thinking about what's possible, thinking about where things are going. Is there anything that you could recommend to people listening to get better at the skill? Because for a lot of product people, this is really important to figure out, where could we be going and let's work back.
turns.zh: 我想再深入探讨一下如何善于提出这些假设性问题。感觉你构建了这样的能力，或者说你天生就具备这种预见未来的技能，能想象可能发生的事，预测事物的发展方向。对于听众来说，您能否给出一些提升这项技能的建议？因为对很多产品经理来说，理解未来趋势并从中倒推策略真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: This is a really interesting question. And I may actually write, I've been thinking about writing a book from some of my Sunday letters, and this is maybe the frame of it. So I'm curious to see how flamed I get from saying this, it'll be interesting to see. I think there's this weird thing that I've noticed. I go talk to university kids and stuff like that, and there's this weird thing I noticed where when I was in university and I would talk to old guys like me, they would all say the PC is this stupid toy, whatever, it's not real computing, go on a mainframe or whatever. And my attitude was like, "Out of the way, old man, just like, you're irrelevant. I'm going to go do this thing. It's awesome." And go, go, go. (00:50:21): And now when I talk to kids, I actually had a slide up at Michigan when I was talking recently that was titled, okay humor, and the professor actually put it up there. Because this generation is very pessimistic and doesn't seem to be quite as engaged and energetic about solving problems. And I've been puzzling through it. And I think maybe there's a bunch of different things that intersect. (00:50:41): I think one of them is, I think they all have to do with the willingness to take risk and to fail, honestly. I think that's really where it comes from. So I think you see a lot of filtered content. And that filtered content presents low probability events like five and six-sigma events as though they were normal. So you see everybody makes $100 million in their startup in the first three months. So if your startup isn't making $100 million, you're an idiot. There's that stuff. There's also, you're living out loud, so when you fail in that context it feels very painful. (00:51:12): But I think there's also for elite students, like people at these elite schools, they're hard to get into. I went to Michigan, "You're kind of smart. Michigan's a good school. You live nearby, go apply to that one." Nothing serious about it, but kids in the elite schools, their lives are highly curated going up to getting into a school like that now, right? Those students like, "I didn't do sports, I didn't do extracurricular. I was just a weird nerd having to be good at math." And so I think there's that as well. If you're highly curated where you've spent a lot of your life thinking, "Everything I do has to have a reason and an output." It's very hard to just mess around and do something that might lead down a surprising path, right? So that's the curation is part of it. (00:51:55): And then I think just in about the mid '80s when I graduated from high school, we stopped letting kids just play on their own, unsupervised outside with other kids. I grew up in this neighborhood full of, it was like the faculty ghetto for this small university my dad taught at, and we just ran wild. It was on the estate of widow of Dodge Motor, founder of Dodge Motor, so we had a couple hundred acres of swamp and fields to go run around in. We did hair-raisingly, dangerous things that my parents never knew about, and really explored and had fun. (00:52:27): I think if you put all those pieces together, I think there's much less of an ability and willingness and skillset around experimenting to the point of failure, making a fool of yourself, having bad ideas. I send stupid emails to Satya at Microsoft all the time where I'm just like, "I don't know what the hell he thinks of me at this point." Because I send him all these goofy ideas. I think he actually gets it and he's like, he likes it, because I don't think people usually do that for him. But I'm just like, "Man, this is..." Then I'll send him an email a week later. I'm like, "Yeah, that was a dumb idea. Sorry about that. I've decided that wasn't a very good one." (00:53:01): But I think you cannot dance if you can't... If you're afraid to embarrass yourself. You cannot succeed if you're afraid to fail. That's just how it is. You have to have that sense of play. You have to have that sense of, it's okay if this doesn't work, I'll iterate on it. I have this personal motto, which is, from error comes virtue. Because I'm a maker, I make stuff. And I fuck it up all the time. I have poor motor skills, so I make mistakes constantly, and then I just figure out how to make the mistake into a virtue somehow. So I think it's a really good skill to have. The saying I took on this year and I really, really like it as my... I never had a personal motto before. I think it might be my personal motto, it's like, virtue from error.
turns.zh:
这真是个很有趣的问题。说实话，我一直在考虑把我周日的信件整理成书，或许这就是个框架。我很好奇说出这番话会招来怎样的批评，应该会很有趣。我发现了一个奇怪的现象。我去和大学生交流时，发现他们对技术的看法和我们这代人很不一样。上大学时，我会和比我年长的人交谈，他们总说个人电脑就是个玩具，真正的计算应该用大型机之类的。而我的态度是：“一边去吧，老家伙，你根本无关紧要。我要去干正事，这太棒了。” 然后就马不停蹄地行动。（00:50:21）现在和年轻人交流时，我在密歇根大学最近的一次演讲中放了一张幻灯片，标题是“幽默”，而且教授还特意把它展示出来。因为这代人太悲观了，对解决问题似乎没有那么投入和热情。我一直在思考其中的原因。（00:50:41）我觉得其中一个关键点在于，人们不愿意承担风险和面对失败。坦白说，这才是问题的根源。所以你看到很多被过滤的内容。那些过滤后的内容把五西格玛这样的低概率事件当作常态。比如创业公司三个月就赚1亿美元，如果你的创业项目没达到这个目标，你就是个白痴。这类例子太多了。还有，精英学校的学生，进入这些名校太难了。我上密歇根大学时，教授说：“你挺聪明的，密歇根是个好学校。你住得近，就去申请吧。” 根本没当回事。但精英学校的学生，从小到大被精心安排，进入这类学校的路径本身就充满条条框框。比如那些学生会说：“我不参加体育活动，不做课外活动，就是个痴迷数学的怪胎。” 这也是原因之一。如果你被过度安排，一生都在思考“我做每件事都要有目的和产出”，要想随心所欲地尝试新事物，找到意想不到的方向，就很难了。（00:51:55）再回想上世纪80年代中期我高中毕业时，我们不再让孩子们在无人监管的情况下和其他孩子一起玩耍了。我成长的社区就像我父亲任教的小型大学的教职员工聚居区，我们可以尽情撒野。在道奇汽车创始人遗孀的庄园里，有几百英亩的沼泽和田野供我们奔跑。我们做过一些惊险又危险的尝试，父母根本不知道。我们真正探索并享受乐趣。（00:52:27）把这些因素综合起来，我认为人们越来越缺乏通过实验去直面失败、承认自己愚蠢、尝试新想法的能力和意愿。我老是给微软的萨蒂发一些愚蠢的邮件，比如“我不知道他现在怎么看我”。因为我总给他发些古怪的想法。他其实能理解，还挺喜欢的，因为别人通常不会这么做。但我就是
比如，“天哪，这真是……”然后一周后我给他发了封邮件。我当时就想，“是啊，这真是个愚蠢的主意。抱歉啦。我意识到这主意不怎么样。”（00:53:01）：但我觉得如果你不敢……如果你害怕出丑，那你就跳不了舞。如果你害怕失败，那你就注定不会成功。就是这么个道理。你得有那种玩乐的心态。你得有种“即使这次不成功也没关系，我会不断改进”的态度。我有个个人座右铭，那就是“从错误中汲取智慧”。因为我是个创客，总是在做东西。每次都会出错。我手眼协调能力差，错误不断，但我总能想办法把错误转化为优势。所以我觉得这真是个很棒的技能。今年我选了这句话作为座右铭，真的非常喜欢……我以前从没有个人座右铭。我觉得这句话可能就是我的座右铭了——从错误中汲取智慧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. On this topic of failing. I think a lot of people hear this advice and they're like, "Yeah, okay, I need to fail more." It's hard to do. And oftentimes your performance at a company is negatively impacted. And it feels like for you it was just, you've done it enough times where fine, okay, it's going to be fine. I launch this thing, no one cares. I email Satya this thing, he ignores it or he doesn't. It's going to be okay. Is that maybe the key to this or is there anything else that you've done to allow you to be okay with failure?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。说到失败这个话题，我觉得很多人听到这种建议时，都会想：“是啊，好吧，我需要多失败几次。” 但这很难做到。很多时候，你在公司的表现会受到负面影响。而对你来说，你似乎已经习惯了这种失败——你已经失败过很多次了，所以觉得没关系。推出一款产品，没人感兴趣。把邮件发给萨蒂亚（Satya Nadella），他要么忽视，要么无视。但没关系。这种心态或许是关键所在，或者你还做了其他什么事情，才能坦然面对失败？

turns.speaker: Sam Schillace
turns.en: I feel like you can have a linear return on your effort if you manage things in a linear way, which is I think that tightly managing, okay, nothing's going to be surprising, I'm going to be within this boundary, I'm going to slowly accrete value, I'm going to play this game, whatever. I think you can have a nice linear, boring return to your career and you'll climb the ladder, it takes 30 years or whatever. I don't have the patience for that. And I think the way you get extraordinary returns is you do extraordinary things, right? You have to take bigger risks, and have more interesting shots to have this kind of extraordinary result in your career. (00:54:56): I feel like I always tell people, I think... I mean, I pitch this because I've observed myself and thought about what has been successful in my career. It's not a thing everybody can do. I'm just kind of like this. I never really fully grew up. I'm kind of this weirdo. I still feel... I'm 57 now, and I feel like I'm about 17. I'm still very immature and like to mess around with stuff and play with things. So not everybody can do it. But I think there's, at the end of the day, the reason you get ahead in your career is you had a lot of impact. And the reason you had a lot of impact was because you picked something that you're good at that you did with a lot of intensity that wound up having impact, right? And so I think the good at part of it is hard too. We tend to undervalue the things we're good at. We tend to think work has to be unpleasant. And so if something is easy and fun, we don't tend to think it's very valuable. (00:55:51): So I think lots of people gravitate in this direction of, let's go do unpleasant things and grind our way through the career, because that's the way to make it. But the reality is, you should go do the thing that you feel guilty to get paid for, if there's a thing like that, and do the hell out of it, right? Do it as hard as you can. If you get pleasure from doing something that people want to pay you for, do it the best you can do it, as hard as you can do it. And if that's messing around and playing around with cool ideas, do the hell out of that. (00:56:19): Work doesn't necessarily have to be hard. It often is, but it doesn't have to be. And the best case is that it isn't. The most impact you'll ever have is where you're in that mode where you're just in the flow and doing your thing and you're happy to do it and you can't quite believe they pay you and you don't understand how you're getting away with this, but it's super cool anyways, right?
